name: Tonsillectomy

lead: A tonsillectomy removes the palatine tonsils from the sides of the throat. In looksmaxxing and bad-breath discussions it is raised as a permanent answer to severe, recurring tonsil stones and the breath odour they cause.

With the tonsils gone, the crypts where stones collect no longer exist. Guidelines recommend the operation for frequent, well-documented throat infections and for sleep-disordered breathing, and it is among the most common operations in children. Medical sources describe it as an option clinicians may consider for persistent bad breath from tonsil crypts when lesser measures fail, while Wikipedia states there is no good evidence for using it for stones or bad breath.

paras: It is done under general anaesthetic using dissection, electrocautery, coblation or similar tools, and recovery takes one to two weeks. It is generally considered only after gargling, rinses and clinic options have been tried.

Bleeding is the most common serious complication, roughly 0.2 to 3.3 percent depending on timing. Throat pain is substantial, especially in adults, and rare deaths are reported. Other risks include dehydration, nausea and anaesthetic complications.

angle.text: Tonsillectomy removes the crypts where tonsil stones form, so people with severe, recurring stones consider it as a last-resort route to fresher breath. Guidelines support it for recurrent infection and sleep apnoea; its use for stones rests on case reports and patient accounts.

lead: Tonsillectomy is the surgical removal of both palatine tonsils, usually under general anaesthesia. It is one of the most frequently performed operations in children, with the main indications being recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep-disordered breathing [1][2][3].

In looksmaxxing and halitosis communities it is mentioned as a definitive option for severe tonsil stones (tonsilloliths), since the stones form in the tonsil crypts. Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence for tonsillectomy as a treatment for tonsil stones or bad breath [2], while a general reference on tonsil stones lists partial or complete tonsillectomy among options that may be considered if bad breath persists [4].
Published guidelines emphasise selective use, because many sore throats resolve without surgery and the operation carries bleeding and pain risks [5][3].
infobox: About 7 to 10 days (full recovery 1 to 2 weeks)

paras: Wikipedia lists recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and sleep apnoea as the main indications, with peritonsillar abscess, PFAPA syndrome and tonsil cancer among others [2]. The Paradise criteria, derived from trials in the 1980s, define frequency thresholds, such as seven documented episodes in one year, for recommending surgery in children [2]. The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery has issued clinical practice guidelines for tonsillectomy in children, most recently updated in 2019 [3][6].
Wikipedia reports that a 2018 UK study of 1.6 million children found about 90 percent of the roughly 37,000 children undergoing the operation each year were unlikely to benefit [2].

Tonsil stones are mineralised debris in tonsil crypts and are associated with halitosis. A general reference lists home rinsing, curettage and laser cryptolysis as lesser options before tonsillectomy, which may be considered if bad breath persists [4]. Wikipedia's tonsillectomy article states that there is no good evidence for the operation for stones, bad breath, swallowing difficulty or abnormal voice [2].

For recurrent throat infection in children, a summary of Cochrane evidence reports about 0.6 fewer sore throats in the following year, with benefits not lasting long and many children improving without surgery [2]. For sleep apnoea, surgery improves symptoms in most children, though a 2015 Cochrane review found no benefit for attention or school performance [2].

For adults with frequent tonsillitis, Wikipedia cites the 2023 NATTINA trial as finding tonsillectomy more effective and cost-effective than medical treatment, with fewer sore-throat days [2]. Evidence for adult use beyond that is described as unclear [2].

Bleeding is the most common complication, with primary bleeding in the first 24 hours reported in 0.2 to 2.2 percent and secondary bleeding, typically 7 to 11 days after surgery, in 0.1 to 3.3 percent; risk is higher in adults [2]. Reported death rates range from about 1 in 2,360 to 1 in 56,000 procedures, roughly a third from bleeding [2]. Other risks include nausea, dehydration, ear pain, taste changes, dental or airway injury and anaesthetic risks [2].

A large 2013 cohort study of postoperative pain across 179 surgical procedures included tonsillectomy among operations producing high first-day pain scores [7]. Throat pain typically lasts one to two weeks, and is generally worse in adults than children [2]. Wikipedia also reports associations, of varying evidence strength, between tonsillectomy and later inflammatory bowel disease [2]; an umbrella review of environmental risk factors for IBD is among the published literature on this question [8].

Techniques include cold dissection with a scalpel, electrocautery, coblation, harmonic scalpel and laser methods, and partial removal (tonsillotomy) is sometimes preferred for sleep apnoea [2]. Registered trials have compared coblation with cold dissection, needle monopolar electrocautery with cold dissection, and intracapsular tonsillectomy in adults [9][10][11].

Evidence includes clinical practice guidelines in 2011 and 2019 for tonsillectomy in children [3][6], a technical report on childhood obstructive sleep apnoea [12], and a 1998 study linking sleep-disordered breathing to poorer school performance in children [13]. A 1982 comparison of surgical rates in New England, England and Norway documented wide regional variation in tonsillectomy use [14]. No clinical study found in the sources specifically tests tonsillectomy as a treatment for tonsil stone-related breath odour.
Registered trials include intracapsular tonsillectomy for sleep apnoea and recurrent tonsillitis in adults and a trial of tonsillectomy and IgA nephropathy outcomes [11][15][16].

Wikipedia traces tonsil removal to descriptions by Celsus around 50 AD, with Philip Physick's tonsil guillotine in 1828 becoming standard for over 80 years and Ballenger's 1897 work favouring complete removal [2]. By the 1930s the operation was very common; in 1934, 61 percent of 1,000 New York schoolchildren had undergone it [2]. US rates fell after a 1978 NIH review found insufficient evidence of benefit, and the operation remains the second most common outpatient surgery in US children [2].
